doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Nightclub culture and road conditions for musicians
summary: Why alcohol took hold: speakeasy origins, long hours, bus trips and segregated lodging, with Ellington and Calloway's railroad cars.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: This is a little off the topic, but so many of the great names have been associated with untimely deaths and jazz seems to have this persona of alcohol and drug abuse. Why did that happen? I mean besides the obvious reasons, you know you’re working in a nightclub, but are there other reasons for it?

Well I mean to me it’s conjecture, I’m not a social historian you know, but as I — I think the musical culture of the 20s, where it started, right, in speakeasies which in turn became nightclubs. Now nightclubs are not, weren’t originally primarily for music, they were places to sell whisky and the music was to lure people in to buy whisky and that’s the atmosphere. So if you were working these incredible hours I don’t think it’s a stretch to get through a night ‘till three or four o’clock in the morning that it’s pretty hard. And I think a lot fell in that way and they’re sleeping all day and the whole thing and they’re on the road, incredible, I don’t know how those people survived those bus trips, particularly the black musicians. Can you imaging working for forty dollars a week riding in the bus and then you get down and there’s nowhere to stay so they had to stay in rooming houses. They couldn’t go in any hotels except there might have been a black hotel here and there. And of course Duke Ellington and Cab Calloway solved that problem. You know how they solved that problem?

With their own railroad cars. Pullmans. Take it off site and they lived in this thing. And it’s an individual matter because there are a number of people who survived all that without — you don’t hear about them.
